steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting JVNV, a Japanese emotional speech corpus with both verbal content and nonverbal expressions. Explain why nonverbal vocalizations matter, why corpora with them are scarce, how we use LLMs to generate the scripts, and summarize our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Nonverbal expressions and nonverbal vocalizations (NVs); their role in emotion and speech processing
- Low-resource problem: few open emotional corpora with NVs; two causes (scripts, NV phrases)
- Our method: LLM-assisted script generation; the JVNV corpus; experiments
- Contributions list
- Release link

    - another (cite) spontaneous corpus from online game chats; annotating position + emotion of all NVs prohibitive
- Our method and corpus
  - LLM-assisted corpus construction to generate emotional scripts with nonverbal expressions
  - seed words from Japanese sentiment polarity dictionary (cite), NV phrases from previous Japanese NVs corpus (cite) -> prompts
  - in-context learning with handwritten exemplars
  - select high-quality scripts with emotion classifier + language model
  - JVNV: professional speakers, Verbal content + Non-Verbal expressions; about four hours, six basic emotions (cite), four native speakers
  - every utterance at least one NV phrase; NV durations annotated
  - supports speech emotion recognition (SER), expressive speech synthesis; explicit NV phrases + durations -> better for NV research
  - experiments: validate method via phoneme coverage, emotion recognizability; benchmark on emotional TTS with discrete codes from SSL model for NVs
  - gap between read-aloud and emotional speech synthesis; NVs make it harder -> new challenges
- Contributions
  - LLM-based corpus construction method for emotional speech with NVs; first to make speech corpus scripts with LLMs
  - JVNV: phoneme-balanced Japanese emotional corpus with verbal + nonverbal expressions
  - objective + subjective experiments validating JVNV

- Release: https://sites.google.com/site/shinnosuketakamichi/research-topics/jvnv_corpus

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Nonverbal expressions, like vocal, facial, and gestural expressions, are important in human communication. In human speech nonverbal expressions are called nonverbal vocalizations (NVs), meaning vocalizations that contain no linguistic information, like laughter, sobs, and screams. These expressions are fairly casual and are usually used in spoken language. One of the most important functions of NVs is conveying affects. Emotional NVs in particular, which are also called affect bursts, exist widely in many cultures. Most previous research on emotional speech ignored NVs, but recent works have shown that NVs can be applied in many conventional speech-processing tasks, including speech emotion recognition and expressive speech synthesis.

There are only very few open-sourced emotional speech corpora with NVs. Most existing work used in-house datasets for experiments, or even bought a commercial corpus of limited size. So further progress on NVs is held back by a serious low-resource problem. We think there are two reasons for this problem. First, it is hard to get proper scripts for an emotional speech corpus. One earlier work reused neutral scripts from an existing speech corpus and asked the speakers to say them with different emotions. This method is efficient because it can use the existing annotations of the original scripts and does not need to consider some important factors for corpus design like phoneme balance. But with neutral scripts it is hard for speakers to say them naturally with the designated emotions when the speech data is collected. Another work collected emotional scripts from social media but could not guarantee that the corpus is phoneme balanced. Another one even employed workers to write emotional scripts by hand, which is costly and hard to scale up. Second, it gets more troublesome when we need emotional scripts with NV phrases. The first work mentioned above tried to do this by encouraging speakers to add NVs when saying the scripts. But because this was not compulsory, not all utterances in that corpus contain NVs. Another work collected a spontaneous speech corpus from online game chats. It is possible to find nonverbal expressions in this corpus, but annotating the position and emotion labels for all the NVs is prohibitive.

- Our method and corpus
  - LLM-assisted script generation: seed words from Japanese sentiment polarity dictionary, NV phrases from previous Japanese NVs corpus -> prompts; handwritten exemplars (in-context learning); filter with emotion classifier + language model
  - JVNV: professional speakers; about four hours, six basic emotions, four native speakers; every utterance has an NV phrase; NV durations annotated
  - good for SER, expressive synthesis, NV research
  - experiments: phoneme coverage, emotion recognizability; emotional TTS benchmark with SSL discrete codes for NVs; gap read-aloud vs. emotional, NVs harder
- Contributions: LLM script generation (first); JVNV phoneme-balanced; objective + subjective validation; TTS benchmark
- Release: https://sites.google.com/site/shinnosuketakamichi/research-topics/jvnv_corpus

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Nonverbal expressions, like vocal, facial, and gestural expressions, are important in human communication. In human speech nonverbal expressions are called nonverbal vocalizations (NVs), meaning vocalizations that contain no linguistic information, like laughter, sobs, and screams. These expressions are fairly casual and are usually used in spoken language. One of the most important functions of NVs is conveying affects. Emotional NVs in particular, which are also called affect bursts, exist widely in many cultures. Most previous research on emotional speech ignored NVs, but recent works have shown that NVs can be applied in many conventional speech-processing tasks, including speech emotion recognition and expressive speech synthesis.

There are only very few open-sourced emotional speech corpora with NVs. Most existing work used in-house datasets for experiments, or even bought a commercial corpus of limited size. So further progress on NVs is held back by a serious low-resource problem. We think there are two reasons for this problem. First, it is hard to get proper scripts for an emotional speech corpus. One earlier work reused neutral scripts from an existing speech corpus and asked the speakers to say them with different emotions. This method is efficient because it can use the existing annotations of the original scripts and does not need to consider some important factors for corpus design like phoneme balance. But with neutral scripts it is hard for speakers to say them naturally with the designated emotions when the speech data is collected. Another work collected emotional scripts from social media but could not guarantee that the corpus is phoneme balanced. Another one even employed workers to write emotional scripts by hand, which is costly and hard to scale up. Second, it gets more troublesome when we need emotional scripts with NV phrases. The first work mentioned above tried to do this by encouraging speakers to add NVs when saying the scripts. But because this was not compulsory, not all utterances in that corpus contain NVs. Another work collected a spontaneous speech corpus from online game chats. It is possible to find nonverbal expressions in this corpus, but annotating the position and emotion labels for all the NVs is prohibitive.

In this paper, to solve these problems, we propose a corpus construction method that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate emotional scripts with nonverbal expressions. The method first samples candidate seed words from a Japanese sentiment polarity dictionary and NV phrases from a previous Japanese NVs corpus, and these form prompts to generate emotional scripts with an LLM. To make the generation better, we use the in-context learning ability of LLMs and add handwritten exemplars to the prompts. Then we pick high-quality scripts with the help of an emotion classifier and a language model. Second, with this method we build JVNV, an emotional Japanese speech corpus spoken by professional speakers with Verbal content and Non-Verbal expressions. JVNV has about four hours of emotional speech data, covering six basic emotions, from four native speakers. Every utterance has at least one NV phrase. We also annotate the duration of the NV phrases in each utterance. JVNV is large enough for related tasks like speech emotion recognition (SER) and expressive speech synthesis. Also, because the NV phrases and durations are given explicitly, JVNV is more suitable for further NV research than existing corpora with NVs. In the experiments we first validate the effectiveness of the corpus construction method technically, looking at phoneme coverage and emotion recognizability. Then we benchmark JVNV on emotional text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis, using discrete codes from a self-supervised learning (SSL) model to represent NVs. We show that there is still a gap between the performance of synthesizing read-aloud speech and emotional speech, and that adding NVs to the speech makes the task even harder, which gives new challenges for this task and makes JVNV a valuable resource for related tasks in the future.

Our contributions are:

- • We propose a corpus construction method for emotional speech with NVs that uses LLMs to generate scripts, which as far as we know is the very first try at making scripts for a speech corpus with LLMs.

- • We build JVNV, a phoneme-balanced Japanese emotional speech corpus with both verbal and nonverbal expressions. We expect JVNV to further advance related work with NVs.

- • We conduct comprehensive objective and subjective experiments to technically validate the effectiveness of JVNV.

- • We benchmark JVNV on emotional TTS and show the challenges of synthesizing emotional speech with both verbal and nonverbal expressions.

We release JVNV at https://sites.google.com/site/shinnosuketakamichi/research-topics/jvnv_corpus.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Nonverbal expressions, such as vocal, facial, and gestural expressions [1], play an important role in human communication [2,3]. In human speech, nonverbal expressions are called nonverbal vocalizations (NVs), which refer to vocalizations containing no linguistic information, like laughter, sobs, and screams [4]. These expressions are relatively casual and usually used in spoken language [5]. One of the most important functions of NVs is conveying affects [6,7]. In particular, emotional NVs, also called affect bursts, widely exist in many cultures [8]. Though NVs were ignored by most previous research on emotional speech [9], recent works have shown the possibility of applying NVs in many conventional speech-processing tasks, including speech emotion recognition [10] and expressive speech synthesis [11,12,13].

The number of open-sourced emotional speech corpora with NVs is quite limited. Most existing work used in-house datasets to conduct experiments [14,12], or even purchased a commercial corpus of limited size [15]. As a result, further progress on NVs is impeded by a serious low-resource problem. We attribute this problem to two reasons. Firstly, it is difficult to obtain proper scripts for an emotional speech corpus. [16] reused neutral scripts from an existing speech corpus [17] and asked the speakers to utter them with different emotions. Such a method is efficient because it can utilize existing annotations of the original scripts and skip some important factors of corpus design like phoneme balance. However, neutral scripts make it difficult for speakers to utter them naturally with designated emotions when collecting speech data. [18] collected emotional scripts from social media but failed to guarantee the phoneme balance of the proposed corpus. [19] even employed workers to write emotional scripts manually, which is costly and difficult to scale up. Secondly, things become more troublesome when we need emotional scripts with NV phrases. [16] tried to accomplish this by encouraging speakers to add NVs when they uttered the scripts, but since this was not compulsory, not all utterances of the corpus contain NVs. [20] collected a spontaneous speech corpus from online game chats. Though nonverbal expressions can be found in this corpus, annotating the position and emotion labels of all NVs is prohibitive.

In this paper, to solve the above problems, we propose a corpus construction method assisted by large language models (LLMs) to generate emotional scripts with nonverbal expressions. The proposed method first samples candidate seed words from a Japanese sentiment polarity dictionary [21] and NV phrases from a previous Japanese NVs corpus [22] to form prompts for generating emotional scripts with an LLM. To improve generation quality, we leverage the in-context learning ability of LLMs by adding handwritten exemplars to the prompts. We then select high-quality scripts with the help of an emotion classifier and a language model. Second, based on the proposed method, we construct JVNV, an emotional Japanese speech corpus uttered by professional speakers with Verbal content and Non-Verbal expressions. JVNV consists of about four hours of emotional speech data covering six basic emotions [23] from four native speakers. Every utterance has at least one NV phrase, and we also annotate the duration of the NV phrases in each utterance. JVNV is large enough to support relevant tasks like speech emotion recognition (SER) and expressive speech synthesis. Besides, since the phrases and durations of NVs are provided explicitly, JVNV is more suitable for further research on NVs than existing corpora with NVs. In the experiments, we first technically validate the effectiveness of the proposed corpus construction method in terms of phoneme coverage and emotion recognizability. We then benchmark JVNV on emotional text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis, using discrete codes obtained from a self-supervised learning (SSL) model to represent NVs. We show that a gap still exists between the performance of synthesizing read-aloud speech and emotional speech, and that adding NVs makes the task even harder, which brings new challenges and makes JVNV a valuable resource for relevant tasks in the future.

The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows:

- • We propose a corpus construction method for emotional speech with NVs using LLMs for script generation, which is, to our best knowledge, the very first attempt at making scripts for a speech corpus with LLMs.

- • We construct JVNV, a phoneme-balanced Japanese emotional speech corpus with both verbal and nonverbal expressions, which is expected to further advance relevant work on NVs.

- • We conduct comprehensive objective and subjective experiments to technically validate the effectiveness of JVNV.

- • We benchmark JVNV on emotional TTS and show the challenges of synthesizing emotional speech with both verbal and nonverbal expressions.

We release JVNV at https://sites.google.com/site/shinnosuketakamichi/research-topics/jvnv_corpus.
